The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, also known as Chavismo Venezuela was the Venezuelan state between 1999 and 2026. During this time period, the country was under the leadership of the left-wing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV) and its antecedent, the Fifth Republic Movement (MVR), under the ideology of Chavismo. Especially towards the end of its lifespan, the state was widely characterized as authoritarian.
The roots of the establishment of the state go back to the late 20th century. A poor economy in the 1980s and 1990s precipitated a wave of political instability in what was then simply known as the Republic of Venezuela. This included deadly riots in 1989, two successive coup attempts in February and November of 1992, and  of President Carlos Andrés Pérez in 1993. The resulting collapse in confidence in establishment parties resulted in the rise of Hugo Chávez and his eponymous Chavismo movement in the late 1990s. Chávez, the leader of the February 1992 coup attempt, was elected president in the 1998 election, initiating the Bolivarian revolution. A constitutional convention in 1999 resulted in the adoption of a new constitution that formally changed the name of the country to the "Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela," to emphasize the Chavismo claim of imitating Simón Bolívar and his style of politics.
Under the left-wing MVR, and its successor party, the PSUV, Venezuela enjoyed a brief era of prosperity in the 2000s. Venezuela, which has always been a resource-based economy, was able to bolster its social welfare state off the back of high oil-prices during the decade, which led to a temporary decrease in poverty and Chávez becoming popular both domestically, and to a lesser extent, internationally. However, the collapse of global resource prices following the 2008 financial crisis and ensuing Great Recession resulted in poverty swelling within the country by the time of Chávez's death in 2013. Nicolás Maduro succeeded Chávez in a presidential election held that year that was widely accused of being fraudulent, prompting a wave of civil unrest against the Chavismo regime that would last until its end. The country entered into recession in 2014, made worse by a further drop in oil prices concurrently.
In 2017, Maduro called for a constituent assembly that would draft a new constitution to replace the 1999 constitution. The assembly, composed of unelected members, and allowing Maduro to stay in power during the interregnum and skip the 2018 presidential elections, was widely recognized as an attempt to stay in power indefinitely, with many countries declining to recognize it. The 2018 elections, called four months prematurely and largely cited as having numerous irregularities, prompted a political crisis in which opposition leader Juan Guaidó was proclaimed winner by the National Assembly. The crisis culminated in a failed uprising by civilians and parts of the military in 2019, seeking to install Guaidó. In the 2024 presidential election, María Corina Machado, who would go on to win the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, would be declared the winner by outside observers, however, the Chavista government claimed Maduro won by a thin majority, prompting another political crisis.
After the post-Great recession drop in oil prices, beginning in the 2010s, Venezuela suffered under a severe socioeconomic crisis, largely stemming from governmental mismanagement and corruption. The country was gripped with crippling water, food, power, and medical shortages, compounded with major hyperinflation. Disease, mortality rates, and crime skyrocketed. Sanctions applied towards the end of the regime's lifespan by other countries in the New World (including the United States) and Europe worsened the situation. By 2017, hunger had escalated to the point where almost 75% of the population had lost an average of over 19lbs and more than half did not have enough income to meet their basic food needs. At the time of the regime's toppling, 9 million people; roughly 30% of the Venezuelan population, had emigrated outwards due to the crisis.
Ideologically left-wing, Chávez and Maduro pursued an internationalist and anti-American foreign policy, pursuing close ties with Communist Cuba, and, for a time, other leftist governments across Latin America and the world. Its staunch opposition to the United States made it an ally of Russia and China, especially towards the regime's end. Compounded with the increasing autocratization of Venezuela under the Chavistas, and allegations of Venezuela becoming a narcostate due to the proliferation of (often state) Venezuelan influence in the drug trade, led to relations with the United States tarnishing, especially during Maduro's tenure. The United States stopped recognizing Maduro as the legitimate Venezuelan president in 2019, and in 2020, he was indicted on charges including narcoterrorism conspiracy and drug trafficking. Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores were captured by U.S forces on January 3, 2026, following a months-long military buildup off the Venezuelan coast. Delcy Rodríguez, vice president since 2018, has served as acting president since.
